interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is each ball's momentum arrow changing in the hit while the nose-to-tail total arrow beside the table stays exactly the same, when you pull back and play a shot.
interactive.title: The pool table
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fourteen small screens on a pool table seen from above. Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each ball carries an arrow for its momentum, before the hit and after it. Beside the table, the arrows are added nose to tail into one total arrow. It is drawn once for before and once for after. A bounce slider runs from ideal bouncy to sticky. A kinetic energy bar shows the total for all the balls, before and after. A heavy-ball switch makes one ball heavy. Drag the cue ball's aim. Then pull back for speed and let go to play the shot. Pull-back speeds run from 0.5 to 4.0 m/s in steps of 0.5 m/s. Each ball is an example 0.2 kg. The heavy ball is 0.4 kg. Here is the rule the picture follows. A ball's momentum is its mass × its velocity, in kg m/s. Its arrow points the way the ball moves and grows with its momentum. Take one way as positive. A ball going the other way then has negative momentum. During a hit, the two balls push on each other equally hard, in opposite directions, for the same time. So one ball's gain in momentum is the other's loss. The total arrow is the same before and after. The bounce slider sets how fast the balls part compared with how fast they met. At ideal bouncy they part as fast as they met. At sticky they do not part at all. They move off as one. A ball's kinetic energy is ½mv². The bar adds up every ball's. Only at ideal bouncy does it end as long as it started. On a glancing hit, the balls push each other along the line joining their centres. So the struck ball leaves along that line. Each arrow then splits into a part along the cue ball's first line and a part across it. The parts in each direction keep their own total. The screens, in order. Screen 1, do, What does the cue ball do?: two equal balls, the bounce slider at ideal bouncy, the arrows hidden. The cue ball rolls at 2.0 m/s straight at the middle of a still ball. "Two equal balls, set to ideal bouncy. A cue ball at 2.0 m/s hits a still one dead centre. What does the cue ball do?" Choices, in a column: It stops, and the other ball goes on at its speed (right); Both roll on together at half speed; It bounces back the way it came. Hint on Both roll on together at half speed: "That is what balls do when they stick. These are set to ideal bouncy." Hint on It bounces back the way it came: "Then the struck ball would leave faster than the cue ball came in. It would have more energy than the shot had." Read: "Two equal balls are set to ideal bouncy. A cue ball at 2.0 m/s hits a still one dead centre. What does the cue ball do?" Why: each ball is an example 0.2 kg. Before the hit, the shot carries 0.2 × 2.0 = 0.4 kg m/s of momentum. It also carries ½ × 0.2 × 2.0² = 0.4 J of kinetic energy. The struck ball leaving at 2.0 m/s carries both, exactly. Rolling on together at 1.0 m/s keeps the 0.4 kg m/s but only 0.2 J. An ideal bouncy hit keeps both. So the cue ball stops dead. After Check the shot plays and the cue ball stops. Screen 2, show, Momentum has a direction: two equal balls rolling towards each other, each with its momentum arrow, and beside the table the two arrows added nose to tail. Words: "A ball's momentum is its mass × its velocity, in kg m/s. Velocity has a direction, so momentum has one too. Call one way positive. Then a ball going the other way has negative momentum." Then "Pull back either ball." Read: "A 0.2 kg ball at 2.0 m/s to the right carries +0.4 kg m/s. An equal ball at 1.5 m/s to the left carries −0.3 kg m/s. Nose to tail, the arrows total 0.1 kg m/s to the right." Screen 3, do, typed, The total: a 0.4 kg ball rolling right and a 0.2 kg ball rolling left, with their arrows, and the total arrow showing "?". "Take right as positive. A 0.4 kg ball rolls right at 2.0 m/s. A 0.2 kg ball rolls left at 3.0 m/s. What is their total momentum?" A typed answer: 0.2 kg m/s, to one decimal place. Slips: 1.4 kg m/s, "You added the sizes. The ball rolling left counts as negative."; −0.2 kg m/s, "Right is positive here. The heavier ball's arrow is the longer one." Hint: "Give each ball's momentum its sign, then add." Why: 0.4 × 2.0 = 0.8 kg m/s to the right. 0.2 × 3.0 = 0.6 kg m/s to the left. That is −0.6 kg m/s. The total is 0.8 − 0.6 = 0.2 kg m/s, to the right. The total arrow shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 4, show, The total survives: the shot from screen 1, with every arrow showing. Words: "In a hit, each ball's momentum changes. The total does not. The two balls push on each other equally hard, in opposite directions, for the same time. So what one ball loses, the other gains. That holds while nothing outside pushes." Then "Pull back and play a shot." Read: "The cue ball's arrow shrinks to nothing as the struck ball's arrow grows to the same length. For a 2.0 m/s shot, the total arrow beside the table stays at 0.4 kg m/s forward." Screen 5, do, typed, They stick: the heavy ball as the cue ball, the bounce slider at sticky. "A 0.4 kg ball at 3.0 m/s hits a still 0.2 kg ball. They stick together. How fast do they move off?" A typed answer: 2.0 m/s, to one decimal place. Slips: 1.5 m/s, "You halved the speed. Divide the momentum by the joined mass instead."; 6.0 m/s, "They move as one, so divide by both masses together." Hint: "Find the momentum before. Then divide it by the joined mass." Why: before the hit, 0.4 × 3.0 = 1.2 kg m/s. After it, the joined 0.6 kg carries the same 1.2 kg m/s. So it moves at 1.2 ÷ 0.6 = 2.0 m/s. The speed readout shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 6, show, Energy is not kept: the same sticking hit, with the kinetic energy bar. Words: "Kinetic energy, ½mv², behaves differently. In a hit, some of it goes into squashing the balls. A perfectly springy ball would give it all back. These balls stick. So 1.8 J before becomes 1.2 J after. The other 0.6 J leaves as heat and sound. The momentum total stays 1.2 kg m/s." Then "Slide the bounce from ideal bouncy to sticky." Read: "At ideal bouncy, the kinetic energy bar ends as long as it started. Towards sticky, it ends shorter. At sticky, it ends a third shorter. The total momentum arrow is the same at every setting." Screen 7, do, typed, Energy lost: two equal balls, the bounce slider at sticky, the kinetic energy bar showing "?" after. "A 0.2 kg ball at 4.0 m/s hits an equal still ball, and they stick. How much kinetic energy is lost?" A typed answer: 0.8 J, to one decimal place. Slips: 0 J, "Momentum is kept, but kinetic energy is not. Work out the speed after first."; 1.6 J, "That is all of it. The joined balls still move."; 1.2 J, "Both balls move after the hit. Count the kinetic energy of all 0.4 kg." Hint: "Find the speed after from the momentum. Then compare the kinetic energies." Why: the momentum is 0.2 × 4.0 = 0.8 kg m/s. So the joined 0.4 kg moves at 0.8 ÷ 0.4 = 2.0 m/s. Before, ½ × 0.2 × 4.0² = 1.6 J. After, ½ × 0.4 × 2.0² = 0.8 J. So 1.6 − 0.8 = 0.8 J is lost. That is half of it. The bar after shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 8, show, Light into heavy: the heavy ball as the struck ball, the bounce slider at ideal bouncy. Words: "On a bouncy enough hit, a light ball comes back off a heavier one. Its arrow points backwards. So its momentum is negative. The heavy ball then carries more forward momentum than the whole shot had. The total still comes out the same." Then "Flip the heavy-ball switch and play a shot." Read: "A 0.2 kg ball at 3.0 m/s hits a still 0.4 kg ball. The light ball comes back at 1.0 m/s, carrying −0.2 kg m/s. The heavy ball leaves at 2.0 m/s, carrying 0.8 kg m/s. The total, 0.6 kg m/s forward, is what the shot started with." Screen 9, do, typed, Bounce back: the heavy ball as the struck ball, the bounce slider part way, the heavy ball's speed showing "?". "A 0.2 kg ball at 3.0 m/s hits a still 0.4 kg ball. It comes back at 0.6 m/s. How fast does the 0.4 kg ball move off?" A typed answer: 1.8 m/s, to one decimal place. Slips: 1.2 m/s, "The light ball came back, so its momentum after is negative."; 1.5 m/s, "The light ball still moves after the hit. Count its momentum too." Hint: "Give the light ball's momentum after the hit its minus sign." Why: before, 0.2 × 3.0 = 0.6 kg m/s. After, the light ball carries 0.2 × 0.6 = 0.12 kg m/s backwards. That is −0.12 kg m/s. The heavy ball must carry 0.6 + 0.12 = 0.72 kg m/s. So it moves at 0.72 ÷ 0.4 = 1.8 m/s. The heavy ball's speed shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 10, show, Glancing hits: two equal balls, ideal bouncy, the cue ball aimed off-centre. Each arrow after the hit splits into its part along the cue ball's first line and its part across it. Words: "On a glancing hit, split each arrow into a part along the cue ball's first line and a part across it. Each direction keeps its own total. Before the hit, nothing moves across. So after it, the across parts cancel." Then "Drag the aim off-centre and play a shot." Read: "A 0.2 kg cue ball at 2.0 m/s carries 0.4 kg m/s along its line. It leaves at 1.73 m/s, 30° to one side. The struck ball leaves at 1.00 m/s, 60° to the other side. Along the line, 0.3 + 0.1 = 0.4 kg m/s. Across it, 0.17 kg m/s one way cancels 0.17 kg m/s the other." Screen 11, do, typed, Along the line: two equal balls, the struck ball's path drawn at 60° to the cue ball's first line, the cue ball's along part showing "?". "A 0.2 kg cue ball at 3.0 m/s hits an equal still ball off-centre. The struck ball leaves at 1.5 m/s, 60° from the cue ball's first line. How fast does the cue ball now move along that line?" A typed answer: 2.25 m/s, to two decimal places. Slips: 1.5 m/s, "Only the struck ball's along part counts. That is 1.5 × cos 60°."; 1.70 m/s, "That takes away the across part. Along the line, use cos 60°." Hint: "The masses are equal. So compare the along parts of the speeds." Why: along the line, the cue ball had 3.0 m/s. The struck ball's along part is 1.5 × cos 60° = 0.75 m/s. The masses are equal. So the cue ball keeps 3.0 − 0.75 = 2.25 m/s along the line. Its across part is 1.5 × sin 60° = 1.30 m/s. It points the other way, to cancel the struck ball's. The along part shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 12, do, mixed, typed, The cannon: a cannon on wheels seen from the side, a ball leaving its muzzle with its arrow, and the cannon's arrow pointing back. "A 96 kg cannon stands still on smooth, level ground. It fires a 4.0 kg ball at 120 m/s. How fast does the cannon roll back?" A typed answer: 5.0 m/s, to one decimal place. Slips: 120 m/s, "The cannon is far heavier than the ball, so it moves far slower."; 4.8 m/s, "Only the cannon rolls back. Divide by its 96 kg alone."; 0 m/s, "The total stays zero. That needs the cannon to move back." Hint: "The total before is zero, so the two momenta after must cancel." Why: before firing, nothing moves. So the total is zero. The ball carries 4.0 × 120 = 480 kg m/s forward. So the cannon carries 480 kg m/s back. It moves at 480 ÷ 96 = 5.0 m/s. The cannon's speed shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 13, do, mixed, Which cannot happen?: two equal 0.2 kg balls, the cue ball at 2.0 m/s heading for the still one dead centre. "Which of these can never happen?" Choices, in a column: The cue ball stops, the struck ball leaves at 2.0 m/s; The cue ball rolls on at 0.5 m/s, the struck ball at 1.5 m/s; The cue ball rolls on at 0.5 m/s, the struck ball at 1.0 m/s (right); Both roll on together at 1.0 m/s. Hint on the first: "Total each ball's momentum after. That one keeps 0.4 kg m/s." Hint on the second: "Its total is 0.1 + 0.3 = 0.4 kg m/s. Some kinetic energy is lost. A real hit allows that." Hint on the fourth: "That is a sticking hit. And 0.4 × 1.0 = 0.4 kg m/s." Read: "A 0.2 kg cue ball at 2.0 m/s hits an equal still ball dead centre. Which of these four outcomes can never happen?" Why: before the hit, the total is 0.2 × 2.0 = 0.4 kg m/s. The third outcome totals 0.2 × 0.5 + 0.2 × 1.0 = 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3 kg m/s. Nothing outside pushed, so the total cannot fall. That outcome cannot happen. The other three all keep 0.4 kg m/s. Screen 14, do, mixed, typed, Coupling wagons: two railway wagons on a level track rolling towards each other, each with its arrow, the speed after showing "?". "A 30 t wagon rolls right at 2.0 m/s. A 20 t wagon rolls left at 1.0 m/s. They meet and couple. How fast do they move on together?" A typed answer: 0.8 m/s, to one decimal place. Slips: 1.6 m/s, "The wagon rolling left counts as negative."; 1.3 m/s, "You divided by the 30 t wagon alone. Coupled, they move as one 50 t."; 2.0 m/s, "You divided by the 20 t wagon alone. Coupled, they move as one 50 t." Hint: "Take right as positive, and give the left-rolling wagon a minus sign." Why: 30 000 kg × 2.0 m/s = 60 000 kg m/s to the right. 20 000 kg × 1.0 m/s = 20 000 kg m/s to the left. The total is 60 000 − 20 000 = 40 000 kg m/s, to the right. Divided by 50 000 kg, that is 0.8 m/s to the right. The speed shows "?" until the answer is checked.
interactive.ignores: Time is slowed down. Each arrow's length is drawn in proportion to its momentum. The balls slide without spin. The cloth's drag is left out. Over the short time of a hit, the cloth's push is tiny beside the balls' push on each other. So each hit is treated as closed. A cushion is an outside push. So a ball coming off a cushion changes the total. The picture stops before any ball reaches one. Real pool balls are nearly bouncy, never perfectly. So the ideal bouncy end is an ideal. On a glancing hit, the balls are taken as perfectly smooth. So they push only along the line joining their centres. Real balls grip a little and set each other spinning. Every mass and speed is an example figure, not a real ball's or wagon's.

explain.text:
When things collide with no outside push, their total momentum stays the same. Each one's share changes. Kinetic energy may be lost. The momentum total is not.

A ball's momentum is its mass × its velocity, in kg m/s. Velocity has a direction, so momentum has one too. Pick one way as positive. A ball going the other way then counts as negative. Now think about the hit itself. Each ball pushes on the other. By Newton's third law, the two pushes are equal and opposite. They also last exactly as long. Each ball touches the other only while the other touches it. So whatever momentum one ball gains, the other loses. Only an outside push, such as a cushion or a hand, can change the total. A set of things with no outside push is a [[closed system]].[^1] In a closed system, total momentum before a hit equals total momentum after.[^2] On the pool table, each ball's arrow changes in the hit. The total arrow beside the table does not.

Try it with numbers. A 0.4 kg ball at 3.0 m/s hits a still 0.2 kg ball. They stick. Before, the momentum is 0.4 × 3.0 = 1.2 kg m/s. After, the joined 0.6 kg carries the same 1.2 kg m/s. So it moves at 1.2 ÷ 0.6 = 2.0 m/s. Now work out the kinetic energy, ½mv². Before, ½ × 0.4 × 3.0² = 1.8 J. After, ½ × 0.6 × 2.0² = 1.2 J. So 0.6 J has gone from the movement. Here is why energy can go when momentum cannot. In the hit, some movement energy goes into squashing the balls. A perfectly springy ball would give it all back as it springs out. These balls stick. So part of it ends up as heat and sound. The pushes still give equal and opposite momentum. So the momentum total stays the same.[^3]

A hit that keeps all the kinetic energy is an [[elastic collision]]. One that loses some is an [[inelastic collision]]. A sticking hit loses the most kinetic energy. Neither quantity has to stay the same for each ball. With no outside push, the whole set keeps its momentum total in every hit. It keeps its kinetic energy total only in an elastic collision.

On a glancing hit, split each momentum into a part along the first line and a part across it. The pushes are equal and opposite. So their parts in any direction are too. So each direction keeps its own total. The ideal bouncy hit is a teaching model. Real pool balls lose a little kinetic energy in every hit. **With no outside push, total momentum before a hit equals total momentum after, even when kinetic energy is lost.**

analogy.text: Connect a charged capacitor across an equal, empty one. Charge flows until both sit at the same voltage. The total charge is kept, just like the momentum total. But the stored energy, ½CV², falls to half. The lost half goes mostly as heat in the wiring. Two equal balls do the same when one hits the other at rest and they stick. They keep their momentum and lose half their kinetic energy.
analogy.breaks: Charge has a sign but no direction in space. So there is no glancing version with along and across parts. Through a plain wire, the two capacitors always end at one voltage, like balls that stick. There is no bouncy version where all the energy comes back.

practice.text:
- Around moving loads or wagons, keep clear. Follow the site's safe system of work first. These sums describe a hit. They do not make one safe.
- Sketch the set-up before and after the hit. Pick one direction as positive.
- Put every mass in kg and every speed in m/s.
- Write each momentum as mass × velocity, with its sign.
- Set the total before equal to the total after. Then solve for the unknown.
- If things join, they share one velocity. So use their total mass.
- On a glancing hit, do one sum along the first line. Do a separate one across it.
- Check the kinetic energy. After a hit, it cannot be more than before. The exception is when something like a spring or an explosion adds energy.
- Read the answer's sign. A minus means the other way.

**Rule of thumb:** with no outside push, the momentum total is kept in every hit. The kinetic energy total is kept only in an ideal bouncy one. Two equal balls in an ideal bouncy head-on hit swap velocities.

**Worked example:** a 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s runs into a still 1 kg trolley. They couple. Momentum before: 2 × 3 = 6 kg m/s. After, 3 kg carries the same 6 kg m/s. So it moves at 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s. Kinetic energy before: ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J. After: ½ × 3 × 2² = 6 J. So 3 J went into heat, sound and the coupling.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding momenta as plain sizes. The other direction counts as negative.
- Expecting each object to keep its own momentum or its own kinetic energy.
- Dividing by one mass when the objects join.
- Writing the unit as kg/m/s or kg m/s². It is kg m/s.
- Mixing momentum up with moment. A moment turns things. Momentum is mass × velocity.
- Calling momentum a force. A push changes an object's momentum. Momentum is what the moving object carries.
- Assuming kinetic energy is kept because momentum is.
